description: Composite two-panel figure of room-temperature compression engineering stress–strain curves. Both panels share identical labelled axes: engineering stress [MPa] on the y-axis, 0–2000 in 200 MPa increments, against engineering strain [%] on the x-axis, whose numeric tick labels are not printed; instead each panel carries a horizontal scale bar annotated "5% ε" (spanning one tick interval) at the lower right, plus a legend defining the filled-circle symbol as σ0.2, which is drawn as a marker on every curve. (a) Five curves numbered 1–5 with in-panel key: 1 Fe-15Al, 2 Fe-15Al-2Ti-1C, 3 Fe-15Al-2V-1C, 4 Fe-15Al-2Nb-1C, 5 Fe-15Al-2Ta-1C. Curve 1 (binary) hardens least and almost linearly; the Nb- and Ta-containing curves show the steepest hardening, the strongest terminating just below the 1400 MPa gridline, and two curves show a plateau/knee near 800–900 MPa. (b) Seven curves numbered 6–12 with key: 6 Fe-26Al, 7 Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C, 8 Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C, 9 Fe-26Al-2V-1C, 10 Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C, 11 Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C, 12 Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C. Curves 8–12 harden with nearly constant slope over long strain intervals, one approaching the 2000 MPa top gridline, whereas curve 6 bends over at low stress. Curves in both panels are drawn with successive horizontal offsets, so strain positions are not directly comparable between curves.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress (0–2000 MPa, 200 MPa ticks) versus engineering strain [%] (x tick numbers not printed; a '5% ε' scale bar gives the strain scale) for five Fe–15Al-based alloys in compression: key 1 Fe-15Al, 2 Fe-15Al-2Ti-1C, 3 Fe-15Al-2V-1C, 4 Fe-15Al-2Nb-1C, 5 Fe-15Al-2Ta-1C. Filled-circle σ0.2 markers sit on each curve; the binary alloy hardens least and almost linearly, the Nb/Ta alloys hardest, with a kink/plateau near 800–900 MPa on two curves.

Same axes as (a) for seven Fe–26Al-based alloys: key 6 Fe-26Al, 7 Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C, 8 Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C, 9 Fe-26Al-2V-1C, 10 Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C, 11 Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C, 12 Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C, each with a filled-circle σ0.2 marker. Curves are offset stepwise along the strain axis; the carbide-forming alloys harden at nearly constant rate, one curve rising close to the 2000 MPa gridline, while the binary Fe-26Al curve flattens at low stress.

observations.observation: Both panels plot engineering stress [MPa] on the y-axis (labelled 0–2000 with ticks every 200 MPa) against engineering strain [%] on the x-axis, whose numeric tick labels are not printed on either panel.
Panel (a) shows five curves numbered 1–5, identified by the printed key: 1 Fe-15Al, 2 Fe-15Al-2Ti-1C, 3 Fe-15Al-2V-1C, 4 Fe-15Al-2Nb-1C, 5 Fe-15Al-2Ta-1C.
Panel (b) shows seven curves numbered 6–12, identified by the printed key: 6 Fe-26Al, 7 Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C, 8 Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C, 9 Fe-26Al-2V-1C, 10 Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C, 11 Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C, 12 Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C.

Each panel carries a horizontal scale bar annotated "5% ε" at the lower right, spanning one x-axis tick interval, and a legend symbol (filled circle) defined as σ0.2; the same filled-circle marker is placed on every curve, marking where the 0.2% proof stress was evaluated.

In (a), the binary Fe-15Al curve (1) rises with the shallowest, near-linear slope, while the curves for the Nb- (4) and Ta-containing (5) alloys show the steepest hardening, the strongest curve terminating just below the 1400 MPa gridline.
Two of the curves in (a) display a distinct plateau/knee in the region between the 800 and 900 MPa gridlines before hardening resumes.

In (b), the curves for the carbide-forming additions (8–12) harden with nearly constant slopes over long strain intervals, one of them approaching the 2000 MPa top gridline, whereas the binary Fe-26Al curve (6) bends over at comparatively low stress.

The individual curves in both panels are drawn with successive horizontal offsets along the strain axis (labels 1–5 and 6–12 placed at increasing strain), so the apparent strain positions of different curves are not directly comparable.
The caption states the figure shows engineering stress–strain curves of Fe–15Al-based (a) and Fe–26Al-based (b) alloys tested at room temperature in compression.
The citing text asserts that the plastic deformation of Fe–15Al–2M–1C alloys shows parabolic work-hardening behaviour, typical of most disordered polycrystalline metallic materials (Fig. 2a).
The citing text asserts that the alloys containing Nb or Ta show the highest strengthening effects and that the hardening of the binary Fe–15Al alloy is low and almost linear.

The citing text states that the deformation behaviour of the Fe–26Al–(2 or 4)M–1C alloys (Fig. 2b) exhibits very high strengthening with almost constant hardening rates until a final stage of parabolic work hardening is reached.
The citing text states that despite the lower yield stresses of most Fe–26Al-based alloys compared with the binary alloy, all these alloys exhibit much stronger hardening during plastic deformation.

unreadable_items: x-axis numeric labels for engineering strain [%] are absent in both panels (a) and (b), so absolute strain values cannot be read from the axes; only the '5% ε' scale bar delimits strain
exact end-point / peak stress of each curve can only be judged relative to the 200 MPa gridlines, no data labels are printed
the exact position of each filled-circle σ0.2 marker cannot be converted to a numerical proof stress because the strain axis is unlabelled and the markers are not annotated
